questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What makes a resolver accept a forged answer
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a resolver can be made to accept a forged answer.
questions.stem: Note 12 of the translator log asks why a resolver on a workstation accepted a tampered answer that it should have rejected.

options.text: The resolver accepted any answer that arrived for the name it had asked about
The resolver accepted the answer because it had cached it during an earlier trusted query
options.misconception: assumes a cached answer removes the need to check a new one

options.text: The resolver accepted the answer because the forged record carried a signature from the zone key
options.misconception: believes a forged answer can carry a genuine zone signature

options.text: The resolver accepted the answer because the queried name fell inside a zone it trusted
options.misconception: thinks trust in a zone means any answer for it is accepted

questions.explanation: When a resolver accepts answers on the basis of arrival alone, a forged response is indistinguishable from a real one. Caching and zone trust only help when the signature or the source is actually verified.
questions.hint: Ask what the resolver checked before it believed the answer.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What encrypted name resolution changes about the trust decision
questions.learningObjective: Describe how encrypted name resolution changes the trust decision.
questions.stem: Note 19 of the translator log compares two lookup paths and asks what changes when the query and the answer are encrypted.

options.text: The trust shifts from trusting the zone key to trusting the network path and the server address
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the trust change under encryption

options.text: The trust shifts from trusting the network path to trusting only the server holding the zone key
No trust decision changes, because encryption protects the content but not the source
options.misconception: believes encryption leaves the source of the answer unverified

options.text: The trust shifts to trusting the resolver cache, because encrypted answers cannot be poisoned
options.misconception: assumes encrypted lookups remove the need to consider cache poisoning

questions.explanation: Encrypted name resolution stops the resolver trusting the network path, so the source must still be established cryptographically. Encryption moves the trust, it does not remove the need for verification.
questions.hint: Ask where the trust has moved, not whether it disappeared.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an open wireless network gives away beyond the link
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an open wireless network reveals beyond the link it serves.
questions.stem: Note 33 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of what an open wireless network reveals beyond the single link it serves.

answer.exemplar: A client on an open wireless network sends its traffic in the clear to the access point and onward, so anyone on the same radio can read it. Beyond that immediate link, the network exposes the identifiers the client presents, the names it asks for, and the timing of its activity, all of which let an observer build a profile of the person using the device rather than merely observe one session.

questions.explanation: An open network gives an observer both the readable traffic on that radio and a record of which devices and names appear on it. The lasting value is the profile built from repeated sightings.
questions.hint: Ask what an observer can build over repeated sessions.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What one pre-shared key does not distinguish
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a single pre-shared key cannot distinguish.

stimulus.body: A glossary draft in the translator notes defines a network where every participant uses the same secret to derive keys for the wireless link. A later remark asks what that shared secret cannot tell the participants apart by.

questions.stem: Given the glossary draft in the translator notes, what can the shared secret not distinguish?

options.text: Whether the traffic on the link was encrypted or left in the clear
options.misconception: thinks a shared key leaves the traffic unencrypted

options.text: Which individual participant is on the other end of the link
Whether the device at the other end is authorised to use the network
options.misconception: assumes one shared key still identifies individual members

options.text: Whether the traffic reached the intended destination or was redirected
options.misconception: believes a shared key prevents redirection of traffic

questions.explanation: A single shared secret gives every participant the same key material, so it authenticates the network rather than the person. It cannot say which device is on the other end, only that someone holding the same secret is.
questions.hint: Ask whether the key names a person or the network.

questions.learningObjective: State what the four-message handshake establishes and what it leaves open.
questions.stem: Note 41 of the translator log asks for two facts about the four-message handshake: what it establishes, and what it still leaves open.

options.text: It establishes mutual authentication and key material, and it leaves the network unencrypted afterwards
options.misconception: confuses handshake completion with ongoing traffic protection

options.text: It establishes only one-sided authentication of the server, and it leaves the old key open to replay
options.misconception: believes the handshake authenticates only the server

options.text: It establishes mutual authentication and key material, and it leaves the old key open to replay
It establishes nothing on its own, and it leaves the client free to choose any session key
options.misconception: thinks the handshake produces no key material at all

questions.explanation: The four messages authenticate both ends and agree fresh session keys, so an old key cannot drive a fresh handshake replay. It says nothing about how later traffic is protected.
questions.hint: Ask what an attacker with an old capture cannot do.

options.text: The need for both sides to know a shared secret beforehand
options.misconception: thinks simultaneity removes the need for a shared secret

options.text: The exposure of traffic on the radio while the handshake is running
options.misconception: believes the handshake exchange is protected from eavesdroppers

options.text: The requirement that the access point keep a list of authorised device addresses
options.misconception: assumes simultaneity removes the need for access point filtering

options.text: The chance for one side to impersonate the other during the exchange itself

questions.explanation: In a one-sided exchange the answering side proves nothing, so it can be impersonated. Simultaneous authentication has both sides contribute so neither dictates the outcome alone.
questions.hint: Ask which side could fake the exchange one-sided.

options.text: One management frame carrying a long payload of application data
options.misconception: confuses a management frame with an application data frame

options.text: Four protected data frames that arrive in the same millisecond as the disconnect
options.misconception: believes protected data frames can carry a disconnect request

options.text: One unauthenticated frame that merely repeats a beacon schedule
options.misconception: thinks a repeated beacon pattern signals a forced disconnect

options.text: Four management frames sent from a single source address with no authentication exchange

questions.explanation: A deauthentication frame is an unauthenticated management frame whose only purpose is to end an association. A burst from one address with no authentication exchange signals a forced disconnect.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What encrypted name resolution changes about the trust decision
questions.learningObjective: Explain how verification changes a resolver trust decision.
questions.stem: Note 63 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of what changes when a resolver verifies answers cryptographically instead of trusting the path.

answer.exemplar: Without verification, a resolver believes any answer that arrives for the name it asked about, so an attacker on the path can substitute a record with an address of their choosing. With verification, the resolver checks the signature against the zone key before using the answer, so a substituted record fails the check and is discarded, at the cost of additional queries and a reliance on correct time.

questions.explanation: Trusting the path means accepting whatever arrives, so substitution succeeds silently. Verifying the signature means a substituted record fails and is dropped, which costs extra lookups.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a substituted record under each approach.

questions.topic: What a long-lived verification record buys an attacker
questions.learningObjective: State how long a captured verification record remains usable.

stimulus.body: A glossary draft describes a verification record that stays valid for a fixed period and can be replayed by anyone who captures it, because the record itself carries no proof of who sent it. A remark in the margin asks how long an attacker who captured one can keep using it.

questions.stem: A captured record in the glossary draft can be replayed for how long?

options.text: Only until the next lookup, because the resolver refreshes the record each time it is used
options.misconception: assumes the record is single use and refreshed on each lookup

options.text: Indefinitely, because the record can be replayed with the attacker own copy of the key
options.misconception: believes a captured record can be replayed forever with a copied key

options.text: Only while the attacker stays on the same network segment as the resolver
options.misconception: thinks replay is limited to the segment where it was captured

options.text: Until the record expires, because replaying it does not require any new access

questions.explanation: The value of a captured record lies in it being self-contained and still valid, so an attacker replays it until it expires without needing further access. Nothing in the record identifies who presented it.
questions.hint: Ask what the record needs at replay time besides itself.

options.text: It exposes the traffic in the clear during the session, and it accumulates nothing beyond that session
options.misconception: believes an open network leaves no lasting trace

options.text: It exposes the devices present during the session, and it accumulates a profile of encrypted payloads
options.misconception: thinks the accumulated profile is built from encrypted payloads

options.text: It exposes the traffic in the clear during the session, and it accumulates a device profile
It exposes nothing during the session, and it accumulates a device profile
options.misconception: assumes an open network conceals the traffic during the session

questions.explanation: Traffic on an open network is readable while it passes, and repeated sightings of the same devices and names build a profile that outlives any single session. Neither fact requires special equipment.
questions.hint: Ask what a repeat visitor leaves behind.

options.text: The good traffic from the traffic that should be discarded, because the key encrypts everything alike
options.misconception: believes a shared key separates good traffic from bad traffic

options.text: The individual participants, because every participant derives the same keys from one secret
The authorised devices from the unauthorised ones, because the key is not linked to any device
options.misconception: thinks one shared key still identifies which devices are authorised

options.text: The encrypted sessions from the unencrypted ones, because the key protects only some traffic
options.misconception: assumes a shared key leaves some traffic unencrypted

questions.explanation: One shared secret gives every participant identical key material, so the network is authenticated but the participants are not. It cannot attribute traffic to a person or a device.

options.text: Only the access point sends a value derived from the shared secret, so the client is not challenged
options.misconception: believes the handshake authenticates only the access point

options.text: Both sides send a value derived from the shared secret, so neither can be replayed by a listener
Neither side sends anything, so the exchange carries no proof that both know the secret
options.misconception: thinks the four messages contain no proof of shared knowledge

options.text: The client sends a password in the clear, so the access point can confirm it offline
options.misconception: assumes a cleartext password is exchanged during the handshake

questions.explanation: Mutual authentication appears as both sides proving knowledge of the secret without sending it, which stops a listening device replaying either side. One-sided or cleartext exchanges do not give that protection.
questions.hint: Look for proof from both directions in the exchange.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a deauthentication management frame achieves
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a deauthentication frame is a denial of service tool.
questions.stem: Note 90 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of why a deauthentication frame is a denial of service tool.

answer.exemplar: The frame carries no proof that it came from the genuine access point, so anyone able to transmit on the radio can send it and claim that the association should end. A client that believes the frame tears down its connection and shows no way to distinguish the real access point from the attacker. The result is a deliberate loss of connectivity that costs the attacker nothing more than the ability to transmit.

questions.explanation: The frame needs no proof of origin, so any transmitter can send one and end an association. The victim client treats it as genuine, which makes a cheap and repeatable outage possible.
questions.hint: Ask what proof the frame carries about its sender.

questions.stem: Given the note in the translator log, what did the resolver fail to do?

options.text: It failed to check where the answer came from before using the address it carried
It failed to check the expiry time of the record before using the address it carried
options.misconception: thinks the missing check was about record freshness

options.text: It failed to check whether the name had been queried before using the answer
options.misconception: believes the resolver needed a prior query for the name

options.text: It failed to check that the address pointed at a host inside its own network range
options.misconception: assumes the missing check was about the address being local

questions.explanation: With no signature and no source check, the resolver had nothing to test the answer against, so a forged address was used as if it were genuine. Neither freshness nor a previous query would have detected this substitution.
questions.hint: Ask what the resolver had that could have tested the record.

options.text: It protects the query and the answer from readers on the path, and it does not hide who asked
It protects the query and the answer from readers on the path, and it hides who asked
options.misconception: believes encrypted resolution also hides the client from the resolver

options.text: It protects the answer from readers on the path, and it does not protect the query in transit
options.misconception: thinks the query travels in the clear to the resolver

options.text: It protects the resolver from forged answers, and it does not protect the traffic between hops
options.misconception: assumes encrypted resolution removes the need for source verification

questions.explanation: Encrypted name resolution hides the content of the query and the answer from observers on the path. It does not conceal the client from the resolver it must ask, and it does not replace signature checks.
questions.hint: Ask who must still see the query in order to answer it.

options.text: The ability to change the address inside the record without invalidating it

options.text: The ability to keep presenting a trusted answer without returning to the target network
The ability to sign new records that will pass the same validation

options.text: The ability to make the resolver accept the record for a name it never asked about
options.misconception: assumes a captured record works for names that were never queried

questions.explanation: A captured record is valuable because it stays valid and self-contained, so it can be replayed later from anywhere. Editing it or using it for an unrelated name are separate problems it does not solve.

A repeated sequence of signal strengths recorded at one fixed location

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the four-message handshake establishes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the four-message handshake achieves on a wireless link.
questions.stem: Note 118 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of what the four-message handshake achieves on a wireless link.

answer.exemplar: The exchange lets both ends prove they hold the same long-term secret without sending it, so neither can be fooled by a device that merely replays an old exchange. It then mixes fresh values from both ends into fresh session keys, so the keys used before the handshake cannot be derived from the keys used after it, which is what defeats an attacker who captured an earlier exchange.

questions.explanation: The handshake produces mutual proof and fresh session keys, so an old exchange cannot be replayed to derive current keys. It is an authentication and key agreement step, not a description of later traffic.
questions.hint: Ask what an attacker with an old capture cannot now do.

questions.stem: An attacker with a captured reply in the glossary draft can do what?

options.text: Decrypt all traffic the network ever carried, because the reply carries the traffic key
options.misconception: thinks the captured reply reveals the network traffic key

options.text: Change the network name that the clients display, because the reply carries it
options.misconception: believes the reply can be edited to change the network name

options.text: Add themselves as an authorised device, because the reply proves membership
options.misconception: assumes the reply proves the holder is an authorised member

options.text: Replay it to the side that issued the challenge and appear to be that side

questions.explanation: In a one-sided exchange the reply is derived from the challenge, so replaying it back to the challenger impersonates the side that answered. Nothing in it grants traffic keys or membership.
questions.hint: Ask who is fooled when the reply is sent back.

questions.topic: What an open wireless network gives away beyond the link
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an open wireless network is useful to a non-participant observer.
questions.stem: Note 145 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of why an open wireless network is useful to someone who is not even on it.

answer.exemplar: Traffic on an open network is often sent unencrypted or with a key that every participant shares, so the identifiers the device presents and the names it asks for are visible on the radio. An observer sitting nearby can record those identifiers without joining the network, because the frames that carry them are broadcast and need no membership to be read. Over several days this yields a record of who was present and when, which is useful even though no traffic was captured.

questions.explanation: Identifiers and names are broadcast and readable without joining, so an observer builds a record of who was present and when. That record is worth having even when no traffic content was captured.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What one pre-shared key does not distinguish
questions.learningObjective: Explain what happens when a device sharing one secret is lost or sold.

stimulus.body: A glossary draft describes a small network where every device is configured with one identical secret and the access point keeps no list of member devices. A margin remark asks how the network behaves when one device is lost or sold.

questions.stem: One device is lost or sold in the glossary draft scenario; what then?

options.text: Every other device is locked out until an administrator issues a new secret to all of them
options.misconception: assumes losing a device can be fixed by removing it from a list

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What encrypted name resolution changes about the trust decision
questions.learningObjective: Explain the trade-off that encrypted name resolution introduces.
questions.stem: Note 171 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of the trade-off that encrypted name resolution introduces.

answer.exemplar: Protecting the query and the answer removes the observer who can read both and substitute a record, but it does not remove the need for the resolver to decide whether the answer is genuine. That decision is now made by checking the signature against the zone key, which requires the resolver to hold the key, to keep accurate time so that expired records are not accepted, and to make extra queries to the authoritative server to confirm the record it was given.

questions.explanation: Encryption removes the passive observer but replaces path trust with key checking, which needs the key, correct time, and confirmation lookups. The cost is in the resolver rather than on the wire.
questions.hint: Ask what the resolver now needs that it did not need before.

options.text: Present it to a resolver as though it had just come from the authoritative server
Extend its validity by resigning it with a key they obtained elsewhere
options.misconception: assumes the holder can extend the validity of a captured record

questions.explanation: The record is a self-contained proof that is accepted until it expires, so presenting it again is enough to obtain the answer it describes. It contains no private key and cannot be extended.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a deauthentication management frame achieves
questions.learningObjective: Explain why repeated deauthentication frames keep a client from staying connected.
questions.stem: Note 197 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of why repeated deauthentication frames can keep a client from staying connected.

answer.exemplar: Each frame asks the client to end its association, and the client has no way to tell the request apart from one sent by the genuine access point, because the frame carries no proof of origin. If the frames arrive continuously, the client repeatedly tears down the association and reassociates, and the session never lasts long enough to be useful. An observer on the radio can sustain the interruption as long as the attacker is willing to keep transmitting.

questions.explanation: Because the frames carry no proof of origin, the client obeys them and drops its association. Repeating them turns a single interruption into a connection that never becomes usable.
questions.hint: Ask what the client does with a frame it cannot authenticate.

options.misconception: believes the laptop was the real authoritative server

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the four-message handshake establishes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an early wireless handshake needed more than a password check.
questions.stem: Note 224 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of why an early wireless handshake needed more than a simple password check.

answer.exemplar: A password check tells the access point something the client knows, but it does not tell the client that the network is genuine, and it sends the proof in a form that can be captured and replayed later. The four-message exchange fixes both problems: each side proves knowledge without revealing the secret itself, and the fresh values in the exchange produce keys that a capture of the old exchange cannot reproduce, so the recorded traffic cannot be unlocked later.

questions.explanation: A password check proves only the client and leaves the secret exposed to capture. The four-message exchange authenticates both ends and mixes in fresh values so old captures stay useless.
questions.hint: Ask what a password check fails to prove and to protect.

The listening device is prevented from hearing the shared secret because it is never sent

options.text: The listening device cannot see the derived values because they are encrypted on the radio
options.misconception: believes the derived values are encrypted on the air

options.text: The listening device is unable to associate with the access point at all
options.misconception: assumes the exchange blocks a passive device from associating

questions.explanation: A passive listener can hear every value but cannot produce the matching response for either side, so it fails the check. Encryption of the values is not what stops it.
questions.hint: Ask what a listener can hear but cannot produce.

answer.exemplar: The frames on an open network carry the identifiers the devices present and the names they ask for, and those fields are broadcast for everyone on that radio rather than addressed to the access point alone. An observer therefore needs no credential, no association, and no position inside the building to collect them. Repeated visits turn those scattered identifiers into a timeline of who was at the location and when, which is the useful part even when no payload is ever read.

questions.explanation: Identifiers and names are broadcast and need no credential or association to collect. Repeated sightings build a timeline of who was present, which is the value even without reading payloads.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of forged answers served during an incident.
questions.stem: Note 272 of the translator log counts a substitution incident: 3 of every 20 lookups for a watched name returned a forged address over 10 minutes, with 24 lookups per minute.
questions.explanation: The forged share is 3 in 20, which is 0.15 of the lookups, and 24 lookups a minute gives 3.6 forged answers each minute. Over 10 minutes that totals 36 forged answers.
questions.hint: Work out the forged fraction, then multiply by the totals.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What encrypted name resolution changes about the trust decision
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a resolver must still believe after encrypted name resolution.
questions.stem: Note 277 of the translator log asks for a written explanation of what a resolver still has to believe after encrypted name resolution is used.

answer.exemplar: Once the query and the answer are protected, the resolver no longer relies on the network to be honest about where an answer came from, so it has to rely on the key instead. That means holding the zone key, checking the signature on every answer, and keeping time accurately enough to refuse records that have expired. If the resolver cannot do all three, encryption on the wire changes little, because a substituted answer still reaches the client.

questions.explanation: Protected transport leaves the resolver relying on the zone key, so it must hold that key, verify every answer, and keep good time. Without all three, a substituted answer still reaches the client.
questions.hint: Ask what the resolver must now check on every answer.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a long-lived verification record buys an attacker
questions.learningObjective: State what an accepting resolver can conclude about the presenter of a record.

stimulus.body: A glossary draft notes that a verification record carries a validity period and no statement of who presented it, and that a captured copy is accepted again by the same resolver. A remark asks what the accepting resolver can conclude about the presenter.

questions.stem: The accepting resolver in the glossary draft can conclude what about the presenter?

options.text: Only that the presenter holds a record that is still within its validity period
That the presenter is the authoritative server for the zone in question
options.misconception: believes presenting a valid record proves the presenter is authoritative

options.text: That the presenter is the same party that produced the original record
options.misconception: thinks a replayed record proves the presenter is the original source

options.text: That the presenter has been authorised by the zone holder for that name
options.misconception: assumes holding a valid record implies zone holder authorisation

questions.explanation: The record says the material is valid and nothing about who holds it, so a replay is indistinguishable from the original. Authority and authorisation are separate questions the record does not address.
questions.hint: Ask what the record says about its holder.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an open wireless network gives away beyond the link
questions.learningObjective: State what an open wireless network gives directly and what it lets an observer build.
questions.stem: Note 283 of the translator log asks for two facts about an open wireless network: what it gives an observer directly, and what it allows the observer to build.

options.text: It gives the observer identifiers and names in the clear, and it allows the observer to read all payloads
options.misconception: assumes an open network exposes payload contents as well

options.text: It gives the observer full control of the traffic, and it allows a profile of who appears over time
options.misconception: thinks joining the network gives control of the traffic

options.text: It gives the observer nothing directly, and it allows a profile of who appears over time
options.misconception: believes an open network reveals nothing to a passive observer

options.text: It gives the observer identifiers and names in the clear, and it allows a profile of who appears

questions.explanation: An open network exposes identifiers and names in the clear, which is what lets an observer build a profile of who appears and when. It does not by itself expose payload contents or give control.
questions.hint: Ask what is readable and what can be built from it.
